power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Lumbar puncture (LP) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis are essential for the diagnosis and management of central nervous system (CNS) infections, but LP is underutilised in pediatric patients in high burden settings.

As part of the pre-screening and screening procedures of the SURE+DP diagnostic sub-study of the SURE pediatric tuberculous meningitis randomised control trial we identified this as a key clinical issue and quantified how often pediatric lumbar puncture was performed at recruiting African hospitals and implemented a package of interventions to increase LP rates.
We evaluated the frequency of pediatric CSF sampling of children aged 28 days to 18 years at four urban tertiary hospitals in Kampala, Lusaka and Harare.
We developed a family-facing educational video to support LP consent discussions.

In Zambia and Zimbabwe, healthcare workers received training sessions including mannequin-based LP simulation, with knowledge, confidence, experience and perceived barriers assessed before and after training.
We assessed the effect of healthcare worker LP training on confidence and LP performance and explored reported barriers to pediatric LP.
Median weekly pediatric CSF samples were 1 at both Sally Mugabe and Parirenyatwa hospitals in Harare, 6 at University Teaching Hospital in Lusaka, and 4 at Mulago Hospital in Kampala.
Training significantly improved healthcare-worker self-reported confidence to assist (p-value <0.001) and perform pediatric LP (p-value <0.001).
text.formatted: Training significantly improved healthcare-worker self-reported confidence to assist (p-value <0.001) and perform pediatric LP (p-value <0.001).

text.text: At the Zambian site, the proportion of children with coded diagnoses compatible with consideration of LP who had CSF samples increased by 7% in the six months after training compared with the preceding six months (p=0.002).
In Zimbabwe, there was an increase in LP activity the week following training, which was not subsequently sustained.

Healthcare workers identified parental refusal, limited procedural confidence, delays obtaining consent from male family decision makers, fear of complications, and consumables availability as barriers.

Discussion: Pediatric LP was performed infrequently across these tertiary hospitals, and improved healthcare worker confidence following training did not consistently translate into sustained increases in LP performance.

Multifaceted sustained approaches combining healthcare worker training with caregiver engagement, system level support and improved resources are needed to improve diagnostic LP use for children with suspected CNS infections.
Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is an important cause of severe childhood neurological disease in high burden settings and is associated with substantial mortality and neurological disability (1, 2).
text.formatted: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is an important cause of severe childhood neurological disease in high burden settings and is associated with substantial mortality and neurological disability <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2)</ref>.

text.text: Diagnosis of TBM requires an aseptically collected cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample, obtained by lumbar puncture (LP) in the absence of contraindications.

This sample is analysed by microscopy, biochemistry, mycobacterial and conventional bacterial culture and rapid nucleic acid amplification tests for TB alongside timely exclusion of alternative diagnoses (3, 4).
text.formatted: This sample is analysed by microscopy, biochemistry, mycobacterial and conventional bacterial culture and rapid nucleic acid amplification tests for TB alongside timely exclusion of alternative diagnoses <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">4)</ref>.

text.text: Given it is not possible to reliably clinically discriminate between CNS infections, LP and CSF analysis is the cornerstone of making the correct diagnosis and initiating appropriate treatment for all causes of meningitis.
CNS infections affect more than 1.2 million children annually worldwide, with the greatest burden being in Africa and Southeast Asia (5-7).
Consequently, failure to perform LP when indicated can contribute to diagnostic uncertainty and delayed or inappropriate management (3).
Even in settings where LP has been well established as best practice, its use in routine care is often suboptimal.
Pediatric hospitals in high-income countries have reported declining LP rates, indicating that barriers to LP are not confined to resource-limited settings (8).
text.formatted: Pediatric hospitals in high-income countries have reported declining LP rates, indicating that barriers to LP are not confined to resource-limited settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(8)</ref>.

text.text: In Africa, however, additional patient, healthcare worker and health system level barriers may further limit access to diagnostic LP.

Zambian research has identified factors influencing LP performance including healthcare worker confidence, clinical decision-making, availability of equipment and concerns surrounding the procedure (9).
text.formatted: Zambian research has identified factors influencing LP performance including healthcare worker confidence, clinical decision-making, availability of equipment and concerns surrounding the procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9)</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative work involving Zambian patients, caregivers, doctors and nurses further demonstrated that perceptions of LP, communication between health workers and families, concerns about pain and complications, and wider social and health-system factors may influence whether an LP is undertaken (10).
text.formatted: Qualitative work involving Zambian patients, caregivers, doctors and nurses further demonstrated that perceptions of LP, communication between health workers and families, concerns about pain and complications, and wider social and health-system factors may influence whether an LP is undertaken <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Caregiver refusal is also a recognised barrier.

Studies have reported substantial parental refusal of LP among children with suspected CNS infection and have identified fear, misconceptions and concerns about the procedure among factors contributing to refusal (11) (12) (13) (14).
text.formatted: Studies have reported substantial parental refusal of LP among children with suspected CNS infection and have identified fear, misconceptions and concerns about the procedure among factors contributing to refusal <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(14)</ref>.

text.text: In Africa, concerns surrounding LP refusal have been sufficiently recognised to prompt calls for interventions that better understand and address community and healthcareprovider perceptions of the procedure (12, 14).
text.formatted: In Africa, concerns surrounding LP refusal have been sufficiently recognised to prompt calls for interventions that better understand and address community and healthcareprovider perceptions of the procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14)</ref>.

text.text: Interventions aimed at improving LP practice have shown that this problem can be addressed.
Training-based interventions have shown that LP rates can be improved.
In Malawi, a healthcareworker training intervention raised LP rates for meningitis surveillance at secondary-level facilities (15).
text.formatted: In Malawi, a healthcareworker training intervention raised LP rates for meningitis surveillance at secondary-level facilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(15)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, a multipronged intervention addressing diagnosis and early management of suspected acute brain infections across Brazil, India and Malawi demonstrated that coordinated, system-level interventions, rather than training alone, can improve clinical processes (16).
text.formatted: In addition, a multipronged intervention addressing diagnosis and early management of suspected acute brain infections across Brazil, India and Malawi demonstrated that coordinated, system-level interventions, rather than training alone, can improve clinical processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(16)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that improving LP practice requires attention not only to healthcare worker skills and confidence but also to institutional processes, diagnostic capacity and communication with families.

There remains limited information on how often pediatric LPs are actually performed in routine care in hospitals in Africa, or on whether training-based interventions produce sustained change in busy referral settings.

We sought to evaluate this during the Short Intensified Treatment for Children with Tuberculous Meningitis (SURE) trial, the largest ever randomised controlled trial for the treatment of pediatric TBM, that recruited across sites in Asia and Africa (2).

A nested diagnostic sub-study of the SURE trial, SURE+DP, recruited participants in whom a lumbar puncture was clinically indicated in recruiting African hospitals in Kampala, Uganda; Lusaka, Zambia and Harare, Zimbabwe, and this was integrated into the pre-screening and screening procedures for the SURE trial (2, 17).
text.formatted: A nested diagnostic sub-study of the SURE trial, SURE+DP, recruited participants in whom a lumbar puncture was clinically indicated in recruiting African hospitals in Kampala, Uganda; Lusaka, Zambia and Harare, Zimbabwe, and this was integrated into the pre-screening and screening procedures for the SURE trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">17)</ref>.

text.text: We identified that CSF sampling appeared infrequent when compared to the number of children presenting with syndromes compatible with CNS infection, the population size served, and the high morbidity and mortality settings.
The study was conducted at Mulago National Referral Hospital, Kampala serving over 4 million people.
Recruitment to SURE and SURE+DP started in May 2022 and stopped in early 2023 due to an Ebola outbreak and limited numbers of children with TBM.
The Acute Care Unit, which manages acute pediatric presentations, managed approximately 450 pediatric cases per week during the study period.
Because SURE recruitment had already ended, the LP training and questionnaires described below were not conducted at this site.
University Teaching Hospital (UTH) is in Lusaka which has a population of over 2 million.
Recruitment started in May 2022 and ended in July 2024.
The pediatric outpatient department, which includes both the emergency room and non-acute patients, managed 750 cases per week during the study period.
LP training was conducted in July 2023 (as described below) for doctors, nurses and allied health staff.

We used routinely coded emergency department diagnoses to estimate how many children presented with conditions for which LP might be indicated (tuberculous meningitis, cerebral malaria, meningitis, encephalitis, hydrocephalus, other convulsions, spaceoccupying lesions and other CNS disorders).
Parirenyatwa and Sally Mugabe Hospitals are in Harare, with a population of over 1.5 million.
The study period was identical to Zambia.
In 2025 the emergency department of Parirenyatwa and Sally Mugabe Hospitals managed approximately 150 and 700 pediatric cases per week, respectively.
Emergency department attendances for the study period were not available.
LP training was done in July 2023 (Parirenyatwa Hospital) and August 2023 (Sally Mugabe Hospital).

We quantified the frequency of pediatric CSF samples received for microbiological analysis at urban tertiary hospitals that were recruiting to the SURE trial and its diagnostic sub-study SURE+DP (2, 17).
text.formatted: We quantified the frequency of pediatric CSF samples received for microbiological analysis at urban tertiary hospitals that were recruiting to the SURE trial and its diagnostic sub-study SURE+DP <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">17)</ref>.

text.text: Recruitment took place at four urban tertiary/referral hospitals in Kampala (Uganda), Lusaka (Zambia) and Harare (Zimbabwe).

As part of routine screening, weekly counts of pediatric CSF samples (from children aged 28 days to 18 years) received for microbiological analysis at the hospital microbiology laboratory or sent to external accredited laboratories as part of the study were reviewed to understand how frequently LP was being performed.
Neonates were excluded.
Neurosurgical cases could only be excluded in Zimbabwe.
To support consent conversations with families, an educational video for caregivers was also developed.
Consultation with clinical practitioners from all three participating centres and the wider SURE team, with experience in other African settings informed the narrative and key points.
A pilot version was tested by healthcare practitioners and the video shortened in response, prior to translation into local languages Shona, Bemba, Nyanja and Luganda.
The video was then circulated to all healthcare workers in settings where LP was performed, as a tool to aid LP consent discussions.
In Zambia and Zimbabwe, healthcare worker training was conducted at sites where SURE recruitment was ongoing between June and August 2023.
Participants included doctors, nurses and allied health professionals.
Each training session lasted approximately 4 hours and focused on the recognition, investigation and management of suspected CNS infections.
Practical simulation using mannequins was incorporated to demonstrate LP technique.
Knowledge, confidence, prior experience and perceived barriers to performing LP were assessed using questionnaires administered before and after training.

At UTH, Zambia, where denominator data were available, an independent two-group, two-tailed proportion test compared the ratio of CSF samples received to children with a coded diagnosis compatible with the need to consider LP, in the six months before versus after training.
The diagnoses included were TB meningitis, cerebral malaria, meningitis, encephalitis, hydrocephalus, febrile convulsions, other convulsions, space-occupying lesions and other CNS disorders.

Equivalent statistical comparison was not possible in Zimbabwe, where denominator data were unavailable, or in Uganda, where recruitment (and therefore data collection) had already ended before training began.
Median weekly pediatric CSF samples were 1 at Parirenyatwa and Sally Mugabe Hospitals, 6 at UTH and 4 at Mulago Hospital (Figure 1A-D).
text.formatted: Median weekly pediatric CSF samples were 1 at Parirenyatwa and Sally Mugabe Hospitals, 6 at UTH and 4 at Mulago Hospital (Figure <ref type="figure">1A-D</ref>).

text.text: Overall, training significantly improved healthcare worker-reported confidence to assist and hold a patient during an LP (p<0.001 95% CI [-1.38, -0.39]) and confidence to perform LPs in children of all age groups (p<0.001).
text.formatted: Overall, training significantly improved healthcare worker-reported confidence to assist and hold a patient during an LP (p<0.001 95% CI [-1.38, -0.39]) and confidence to perform LPs in children of all age groups (p<0.001).

text.text: In Zimbabwe, an increase in LP procedures was observed the week immediately post-training but was not sustained (figure 1C and 1D).
text.formatted: In Zimbabwe, an increase in LP procedures was observed the week immediately post-training but was not sustained (figure <ref type="figure">1C</ref> and <ref type="figure">1D</ref>).

text.text: At UTH in Zambia, 919 children had a coded diagnosis compatible with the need to consider an LP while 705 CSF samples were received by the lab during the same period (77%).

The proportion of children who had diagnoses compatible with the need to consider an LP and number of CSF samples increased from 91.6% in the 6 months before training to 98.8% in the 6 months after training (p=0.002).

Healthcare workers reported that parental refusal, lack of confidence among junior staff, delays in obtaining consent from male family decision makers, and concerns over complications or resource availability such as LP needles were the main barriers to performing LP in pediatric patients (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Healthcare workers reported that parental refusal, lack of confidence among junior staff, delays in obtaining consent from male family decision makers, and concerns over complications or resource availability such as LP needles were the main barriers to performing LP in pediatric patients (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Across all four hospitals, pediatric LP was performed infrequently when compared to the number of children presenting with clinical features for which LP might be indicated, even though these were tertiary referral centres actively recruiting to a TBM trial.

This was true regardless of country, hospital size, or whether coded diagnostic denominator data were available, suggesting the pattern reflects something structural about how LP is used in routine care rather than a feature of any single site.
There were, however, obvious differences between settings.

Weekly CSF sampling at UTH and Mulago Hospital, while still low relative to the number of pediatric attendances, was higher than at the two Harare hospitals, where the median number of CSF samples was one for the study period.
Several factors could have contributed to this difference.

Denominator data on emergency department coded diagnoses compatible with LP were not available in Zimbabwe, so it is not possible to state with confidence what proportion of children who might have benefited from LP actually received one.
A second possibility is that CSF samples reaching the laboratory in Zimbabwe may under-represent LPs performed for indications outside the trial.

Nonetheless, the consistency of a low median across two hospitals over an extended period suggests that access to LP, whether relating to equipment, staffing, caregiver consent, or institutional practice, was more constrained in Harare than at the other sites during this period, and this warrants further local investigation.
Thirdly, failure to exclude neurosurgical cases in Zambia could have inflated the number of CSF samples reaching the laboratory since these patients typically undergo repeated CSF sampling.

Training improved healthcare-worker confidence at both sites, but this was not consistently followed by a sustained increase in LP activity, supporting the evidence from both Malawi and the multi-country intervention in Brazil, India and Malawi, that system-level or multifaceted approaches, rather than isolated training, are more likely to produce long lasting change in diagnostic practice for suspected central nervous system infections (15, 16).

text.text: The barriers reported by healthcare workers, particularly parental refusal and delays obtaining consent from male family decision makers, are consistent with earlier qualitative work in the region, and point to the need for caregiver and community-facing interventions, such as the educational video introduced alongside training in this case study, as a plausible complement to healthcareworker training (9, 10).
text.formatted: The barriers reported by healthcare workers, particularly parental refusal and delays obtaining consent from male family decision makers, are consistent with earlier qualitative work in the region, and point to the need for caregiver and community-facing interventions, such as the educational video introduced alongside training in this case study, as a plausible complement to healthcareworker training <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">10)</ref>.

text.text: This community case study has several limitations.
Denominator data allowing calculation of LP rates was based on coded diagnoses and were only available at one of four hospitals.
The post-training observation period was relatively short, there was no concurrent control site, and confidence was self-reported rather than directly observed.
Neurosurgical cases could only be excluded from CSF counts in Zimbabwe, which may affect comparability between sites.
CSF samples sent to external laboratories at family and/or clinician discretion outside of the SURE and SURE+DP studies would not be captured.
Our findings confirm that pediatric LP rates are low in high-burden settings, even at referral hospitals participating in clinical trials.
Addressing low LP rates is critical for timely diagnosis and management of CNS infections, especially given high morbidity and mortality.
Training improved healthcare worker confidence but had limited sustained impact on LP rates.

Embedding routine, low-burden surveillance of CSF sampling, for example via existing trial or laboratory data systems, alongside coded clinical denominator data would allow hospitals to track LP practice over time and identify where gains are, or are not, being sustained.

Caregiver-facing tools that address specific, previously identified barriers to consent, including the role of male family decision makers, may be a useful complement to workforce training and warrant formal evaluation.
WHO meningitis 2025 guidelines and Brain Infections Global Health Network resources provide practical guidance that could support this type of system level strengthening (4, 16, 18).
text.formatted: WHO meningitis 2025 guidelines and Brain Infections Global Health Network resources provide practical guidance that could support this type of system level strengthening <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">18)</ref>.

text.text: Additional strategies include mentorship, repeated training, institutional support, improved supply chains and community engagement to address caregiver concerns.

Finally, replicating this kind of CSF surveillance across additional sites, alongside consistent collection of denominator data, would help distinguish genuinely low LP performance from gaps in how CSF sampling or coded diagnoses are captured.

Even within large referral/tertiary hospitals actively engaged in a large TBM trial, pediatric LP was performed far less often than the burden of CNS infection would suggest is needed, and training alone had limited durable effect.
Efforts to close this gap most likely require combining healthcareworker training with system-level support, caregiver engagement, and routine surveillance of LP practice.
